axis_prompt: Demand validation: someone demonstrably wants this — the proposal shows real users, buyers, or beneficiaries pulling for the thing to exist, with evidence stronger than encouraging conversations.
Rank the proposal's demand evidence on the ladder from 'people said it sounds nice' to 'people already pay, use, or wait for it'; rate the rung reached.
If the team announced the product tomorrow with a signup link, what does the proposal's evidence predict happens?
Audit for polite-interest inflation: friendly feedback and event applause counted as demand for something nobody would sacrifice anything to have.
User-contact depth: the team has actually been with its users — watched them work, heard their words, absorbed their constraints — and the plan bears the marks of that contact.
Count the specific, surprising user facts in this proposal that could only come from real contact; generic personas count against.
Could the team describe a real named user's worst day in detail? Rate how much of the plan is built from such days versus from imagination.
Audit for armchair user modeling: needs deduced from first principles for a population the team has never sat beside.
Distribution plan: the path from built thing to reached audience is engineered — named channels, realistic conversion arithmetic, and effort budgeted for distribution as seriously as for building.
For each channel the plan names, check the arithmetic: audience size, plausible conversion, cost per reached user; rate the channels that survive the math.
The product exists and is good — now walk the plan's own steps to its thousandth user; where does the walk break?
Audit for build-it-and-they-come: a distribution section that is one paragraph of hope after ten pages of product.
Adoption pathway: the plan respects how its audience actually changes behavior — entry points that fit existing workflows, friction fronted honestly, first value delivered fast.
Walk a skeptical median user from first hearing about this to daily use; count the steps where the plan smooths the path versus assumes the leap.
What must a user give up or unlearn to adopt this — and does the proposal weigh that cost or pretend it is zero?
Audit for enthusiast extrapolation: adoption projected from early users who love novelty onto a majority who punish it.
Switching-cost realism: the plan knows what its users would leave behind — data, habits, integrations, relationships with incumbents — and prices the true cost of the switch it asks for.
Itemize what a user abandons to move to this solution; rate whether the offered value honestly exceeds that bill.
Why hasn't the audience already switched to existing alternatives? The proposal's answer to that question is the measurement.
Audit for better-is-enough thinking: a marginal improvement expected to overcome lock-in that only order-of-magnitude gains actually move.
Competitive-landscape map: the proposal knows who else is working the territory — direct rivals, adjacent efforts, and the do-nothing incumbent — described accurately and engaged strategically.
List the competing and adjacent efforts a diligent scan would find; count how many the proposal names and how fairly it characterizes each.
If the strongest competitor read this proposal's description of them, would they call it accurate — and does the differentiation survive their best counter-move?
Audit for empty-field claims: 'no one else is doing this' asserted where a half-hour search finds three someones.
Ecosystem timing: the moment is right for this specific project — enabling conditions newly in place, the why-now answered with facts about the world rather than about the team's availability.
Extract the proposal's why-now argument; rate whether it cites real recent changes — technology, policy, prices, attention — or could have been written five years ago.
Would this project have failed if started three years earlier, and will the window still be open in two? Rate how precisely the plan understands its own timing.
Audit for timing by coincidence: a why-now that is really 'why us, now that we happen to be free'.

Market-size honesty: the addressable population is estimated with discipline — bottom-up from real segments, constraints acknowledged, the difference between everyone-who-could and anyone-who-would respected.
Rebuild the proposal's audience estimate bottom-up from its own segments; rate how far the proposal's number drifts from yours.
Take the plan's most restrictive real constraint — language, geography, technical prerequisite — and apply it: what fraction of the claimed audience survives?
Audit for top-down inflation: a giant number multiplied by an invented percentage standing in for actual reachable users.

Partnership credibility: claimed partners are real commitments — agreements at the right level, incentives for the partner to follow through, and the difference between a signed pilot and a warm intro kept honest.
Grade each named partnership by its hardest evidence: contract, pilot, public statement, meeting, or mention; rate the portfolio's real weight.
For the plan's most load-bearing partner, ask why they need this to work; partnerships resting on the partner's own interest score high.
Audit for logo harvesting: organizations listed as partners whose actual commitment is having once replied.
Network-effect realism: where the plan's value compounds with users, the cold start is solved — value delivered to user one, the chicken-and-egg broken by design rather than by hope.
State what the tenth user gets before the thousandth exists; rate the plan's answer for the empty-room problem.
If growth stalls at fifty users, is the thing still worth having — or does all claimed value live beyond a threshold the plan may never reach?
Audit for flywheel fantasy: virtuous-cycle diagrams whose first turn requires the scale that only the cycle could produce.
Maintenance-burden honesty: the plan prices keeping the thing alive — updates, moderation, dependencies, support — with the ongoing cost owned rather than left as an unfunded afterthought.
Estimate the annual cost of keeping this project's outputs functional after the grant; rate whether the proposal states, funds, or ignores that number.
Eighteen months after launch, who is patching, moderating, and answering — and are they paid by anything in this plan?
Audit for launch-and-abandon design: deliverables that decay into broken links and stale data the moment the funded period ends.
Technical-debt foresight: the build plan distinguishes deliberate shortcuts from accidental ones — quick-and-dirty chosen knowingly where it is cheap to fix later, avoided where it compounds.
Find the corners this plan cuts; rate whether each cut is named, justified, and scheduled for repayment or silently structural.
If this prototype succeeds and must suddenly serve ten times the load, what breaks first — and did the plan choose that breaking point on purpose?
Audit for debt denial: a rushed build plan describing itself as production-grade, or gold-plating where a duct-taped pilot was the right call.
Infrastructure pragmatism: technical choices are sized to the actual problem — boring proven tools where they suffice, novelty only where the mission demands it, complexity treated as cost.
For each technology choice visible in the plan, ask what the boring alternative was and why it lost; count the choices that survive the question.
Rate the stack a stranger would inherit: could a competent replacement operate this in a week, or is it a bespoke labyrinth?
Audit for resume-driven engineering: fashionable architecture serving the builders' interests where a spreadsheet served the mission.
Build-vs-buy judgment: the plan builds only what it must — existing tools, services, and platforms adopted where adequate, custom construction reserved for the project's actual differentiation.
List everything the plan proposes to build; count the items an existing off-the-shelf option covers at a tenth the cost.
For the largest custom component, imagine buying instead: what is truly lost — and is that loss worth the build months?
Audit for not-invented-here spending: engineering budget consumed rebuilding commodities while the differentiating work waits.

Open-source strategy: where the plan invokes openness, the openness is designed — license chosen deliberately, community contribution actually possible, sustainability of the open thing thought through.
Check the open-source claims against the mechanics: license named, contribution path described, maintenance owned; count the claims with machinery behind them.
A stranger wants to contribute or fork this project's output next year: walk their path and rate how far they get.
Audit for openness as ornament: 'will be open-sourced' decorating a plan with no repo, no license, and no intention of accepting a pull request.
Platform-risk awareness: the plan knows whose land it is built on — API providers, app stores, social platforms, cloud vendors — and what happens when the landlord changes the rules.
List every third-party platform this project depends on; rate the damage of each one's plausible policy change and the plan's answer to it.
The critical API triples its price or closes: does the project die, limp, or shrug? The plan should already know.
Audit for landlord blindness: a project whose entire value proposition survives only at a platform's continued pleasure, unexamined.

Regulatory navigation: legal and regulatory reality is mapped — the rules that touch the project known, compliance planned, and the difference between forbidden, gray, and fine understood before spending.
List the regulatory regimes this project touches — data, health, finance, employment, export; count the ones the proposal shows awareness of.
Which single legal surprise most cheaply kills this project — and has the team asked anyone qualified about it?
Audit for ask-forgiveness planning: known regulatory exposure waved off as something to handle after traction.
Localization awareness: where the plan crosses cultures or borders, it adapts — language, norms, infrastructure, and local partners treated as design inputs rather than translation chores.
For each target region, count the local facts in the plan that a desk researcher wouldn't know; local depth is the measurement.
Would a practitioner native to the target context read this plan and say 'they understand here' — or list the assumptions that break on arrival?
Audit for copy-paste globalism: a plan proven in one context projected onto others as if context were a font setting.
Accessibility of output: what the project makes can be used by the people it claims to serve — ability, bandwidth, device, language, and literacy constraints designed for rather than discovered.
Profile the least-resourced intended user — old device, slow connection, screen reader, second language; rate how much of the plan's output actually reaches them.
Whom does the current design silently exclude, and is anyone excluded who the mission statement claims to center?
Audit for accessibility afterthought: inclusion in the mission paragraph, absent from the build plan and budget.
Simplicity of design: the solution is as simple as the problem allows — few moving parts, obvious operation, complexity spent only where it buys mission value.
Count the components, integrations, and concepts a user or operator must hold; rate the design against the simplest version that could work.
Explain the solution to its intended user in two sentences: does the explanation survive, or does the design's complexity leak out immediately?
Audit for complexity as impressiveness: architecture elaborated to signal sophistication where the mission needed a simpler tool shipped sooner.
Prototype existence: something already works — a demo, pilot, draft, or v0 that exists and can be inspected, moving the proposal from theory to extrapolation.
Locate the most finished artifact behind this proposal — link, screenshot, pilot data; rate how much of the promised thing already demonstrably runs.
If a funder asked for a live demo tomorrow, what could this team actually show?
Audit for mockup masquerade: slideware and renders presented in the grammar of working software.
Support plan: humans who use the thing can get help — onboarding, documentation, and a response path staffed and budgeted in proportion to the users the plan projects.
Divide projected users by support capacity in the plan; rate whether the quotient is a service or an unanswered inbox.
A confused user hits a wall in week one: walk their path to resolution through what the plan actually provides.
Audit for growth without service: user projections that rise while support remains one founder's evenings.
Security posture: the project protects what it holds — threat-appropriate handling of credentials, user data, and infrastructure, with security treated as design rather than as an incident response.
Inventory what this project will hold that someone might want — data, access, funds, reputation; rate the protections the plan describes against that inventory.
Assume a moderately motivated attacker targets this project in month three: what do they get, and did the plan see them coming?
Audit for security by obscurity and by hope: sensitive holdings described with no threat model, no practices, and no owner.

Privacy conscientiousness: personal information is treated as a liability to minimize — collection limited to need, consent real, retention bounded, and the subjects' interests weighed above convenience.
List the personal data the plan collects; for each item, ask whether the mission truly requires it and rate the fraction that survives.
Would the data subjects, shown exactly what is collected and kept, consent again — and does the plan ever really ask them?
Audit for data hoarding: collect-everything defaults justified by future usefulness, with consent buried in boilerplate.
Vendor independence: the project can change suppliers — data exportable, interfaces standard, no single commercial dependency that converts the mission into a hostage.
For each vendor in the stack, estimate the cost of switching away; rate the plan by its largest hostage payment.
The most critical vendor is acquired by a hostile buyer: how long until this project runs free of them, using only what the plan provides?
Audit for convenience lock-in: proprietary formats and closed APIs adopted for week-one speed at the price of year-two freedom.

Pricing realism: where revenue is part of the story, the pricing is tested against reality — willingness to pay evidenced, unit economics computed, the free-to-paid conversion treated as the hard problem it is.
Check the revenue arithmetic: price × payers × conversion, each factor sourced; count the factors resting on evidence versus wish.
Who has already paid anything for this or its closest analogue? The answer calibrates every projection in the plan.
Audit for hockey-stick revenue: projections that hit sustainability exactly when the grant runs out, derived from no observed payment behavior.
Community fit: the project enters its community well — norms understood, existing efforts respected, relationships preceding the ask, the team welcome where it plans to work.
Count the community relationships that predate this proposal — collaborations, contributions, standing; rate whether the team is arriving or already home.
If the community this project needs were polled about the team, what would they say — and does the proposal's evidence support that answer?
Audit for extractive arrival: a team parachuting into a community's territory for funding purposes, with relationships listed that the community would not recognize.
